blocks.text: Skin, the outermost layer of the body, gives the first defence against microbes. Its epidermis is 10 to 30 cells thick. The outer layer, the stratum corneum, is continuously damaged and shed; new cells formed deep in the epidermis move up to replace them, and these cells make keratin, a protein that makes the skin tough and impenetrable to microbes.

blocks.alt: A block of skin in section. The outer layer, stratum corneum, lies on top of the epidermis. Below are the dermis, with hairs in follicles, an oil gland, a nerve, blood vessels and a coiled sweat gland whose duct opens at a pore, and the hypodermis of adipose tissue. Brackets mark epidermis, dermis and hypodermis.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.2: Layers of skin (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.2).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Hair, Pores, Stratum corneum, Epidermis, Oil gland, Nerve, Dermis, Sweat gland, Blood vessels, Hair bulb, Adipose tissue, Hypodermis.

blocks.text: Skin also defends with chemicals: oil and sweat glands lower the surface pH to 3-5, acid enough to inhibit the growth of many microbes, and sweat contains the enzyme lysozyme, which attacks and digests the cell walls of many bacteria.

blocks.title: For information
blocks.text: Skin is the largest organ of the vertebrate body; in an adult human it is about 15% of the total weight. One square centimetre of human skin has 200 nerve endings, 10 hairs and muscles, 100 sweat glands, 15 oil glands, 3 blood vessels, 12 heat receptors, 2 cold receptors and 25 pressure receptors.
